parsed_answer.content:
In distributed systems and enterprise architecture, scalability refers to a system's capacity to handle growing amounts of work by adding resources to the system. When designing backend applications, architects primarily choose between two scaling paradigms: vertical scalability and horizontal scalability, both of which heavily rely on the implementation of stateless services. Vertical scaling, commonly known as scaling up, involves increasing the compute capacity of a single machine by upgrading its hardware specifications, such as allocating more RAM to the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) heap, adding CPU cores, or migrating to a larger cloud instance type. While conceptually simple because it avoids the complexities of distributed coordination, vertical scaling hits physical hardware ceilings, introduces significant financial costs at the high end, and creates a single point of failure.

Conversely, horizontal scaling, or scaling out, involves adding more independent nodes or virtual machines to a cluster behind a load balancer. This approach offers virtually limitless capacity and high availability, but it fundamentally alters how application state must be managed. To distribute incoming HTTP requests or messaging events seamlessly across any arbitrary node in a horizontal cluster, the services themselves must be architected as stateless services. A stateless service does not store client-specific session data or local application state in memory between requests. Every request contains all the necessary contextual data, such as JWT authentication tokens, or retrieves its required session state from an externalized, highly available data store like Redis or a distributed database. This decoupling of compute and state ensures that if a JVM instance crashes or a container is abruptly terminated by an orchestrator like Kubernetes, no critical user data is lost, and traffic can be immediately rerouted to any other healthy instance.

items: Stateless service design mandates that JVM heap usage remains strictly transient, storing only short-lived method execution frames, garbage-collected request objects, and thread-local data that is thoroughly cleaned up to prevent memory leaks.

To achieve seamless horizontal scalability, sticky sessions must be avoided at the load balancer level unless strictly necessary, ensuring complete request interchangeability across all cluster nodes.

Externalizing session state to high-throughput data grids like Redis introduces network latency overhead, making efficient caching and connection pooling via libraries like Lettuce or Jedis critical for maintaining low p99 latencies.

Distributed synchronization primitives, such as distributed locks using Redlock or ZooKeeper, replace local JVM synchronized blocks or ReentrantLocks when horizontally scaled instances must coordinate access to shared cluster resources.

parsed_answer.content: A classic trap when migrating from vertical to horizontal scaling is the accidental introduction of local state via static fields, singleton beans with mutable instance variables, or local HTTP session caching. In a multi-node Kubernetes deployment, if Node A modifies an in-memory cache, Node B remains completely unaware, leading to data inconsistency bugs that are notoriously difficult to reproduce. Always audit your Spring beans for thread-safety and ensure shared state is explicitly externalized.

title: Scalability — vertical vs horizontal, stateless services
